We just shipped Outlook sync for [App Name].

It took four months, and two engineers built it. Along the way we dealt with OAuth quirks, calendar edge cases, and the fact that every Outlook account seems to have its own idea of how recurring events should work. Some weeks it felt like we were fighting the calendar more than building the feature.

Now you can connect your Outlook calendar and see your bookings, availability, and changes update in both places automatically. No more double-entry, no more "I thought that meeting was moved."

To everyone who asked for this: thank you for your patience. It's here.

If you try it, I'd love to hear what breaks and what works. That feedback shapes what we build next.

[Link]

rows.plain:
Big news: our scheduling app now syncs with Outlook.

It took four months, two engineers, and more calendar edge cases than we'd like to admit. Recurring events that skip holidays. Time zones that shift mid-series. Permissions that look right until someone tries to book a room. We rebuilt sync logic more than once before it held up the way our customers need.

Why it mattered: a lot of you told us your team lives in Outlook, and asking people to switch calendars just to use a scheduling tool was a non-starter. Now your bookings show up where you already work, and changes flow both ways.

To the two engineers who built this: thank you. Four months of careful, unglamorous work is what makes a tool feel effortless.

If you use Outlook and have been waiting for this, try it out and tell us what breaks. We're listening.

#Outlook #Scheduling #ProductLaunch #Startups

rows.plain:
Most small teams skip design docs. The reasoning usually goes something like this: we're five people, we talk all day, we can just start building and sort things out as we go. And for a while, that works. Everyone holds the whole system in their head, decisions get made in hallway conversations, and the code itself becomes the record of what was decided. Then the team doubles, or someone leaves, or a feature turns out to touch three services nobody expected, and suddenly nobody can remember why the auth layer works the way it does or which of the two competing approaches was rejected and for what reason. The cost of skipping the design phase doesn't show up on day one. It shows up months later, quietly, as rework, as arguments that repeat themselves, and as new engineers who have to reverse-engineer intent from code.

A design doc is not a bureaucratic ritual, and it doesn't have to be a forty-page document that gets approved by a committee. At its best, it's a short, written argument: here is the problem, here is what we're going to do about it, here are the alternatives we considered, and here is why we chose this path over the others. Writing that down forces a kind of clarity that's hard to reach through conversation alone. Vague assumptions become explicit, and explicit assumptions can be challenged before they're expensive to fix. A two-page doc that a colleague reads in twenty minutes can surface a flaw that would have cost two weeks of coding. For small teams, where every engineer's time is a large fraction of total capacity, that trade is especially good.
rows.steered:
Small teams often skip design docs because they feel like overhead. Two or three engineers sit in the same room, talk all day, and assume they know what the others are building. That works until it doesn't. Someone builds a caching layer nobody asked for, or two people write competing versions of the same endpoint, or a feature ships and no one can say why the database schema looks the way it does. A design doc takes an afternoon to write and saves days of rework.

The point of a design doc is not the document. It is the thinking that happens before the first line of code, when changing direction costs nothing. Writing down the problem, the constraints, and the options forces you to notice what you don't yet understand. It also gives teammates a chance to object while objecting is still cheap. On a small team, where one person's wrong assumption can take up a third of the group's week, that chance is worth a lot.
rows.rewritten:
Most small teams skip design docs. The reasoning usually goes something like this: we're five people, we talk all day, we can just start building and sort things out as we go. And for a while, that works. Everyone holds the whole system in their head, decisions get made in hallway conversations, and the code itself becomes the record of what was decided. Then the team doubles, or someone leaves, or a feature turns out to touch three services nobody expected, and suddenly nobody can remember why the auth layer works the way it does or which of the two competing approaches was rejected and for what reason. The cost of skipping the design phase doesn't show up on day one. It shows up months later, quietly, as rework, as arguments that repeat themselves, and as new engineers who have to reverse-engineer intent from code.

A design doc is not a bureaucratic ritual, and it doesn't have to be a forty-page document that gets approved by a committee. At its best, it's a short, written argument: here is the problem, here is what we're going to do about it, here are the alternatives we considered, and here is why we chose this path over the others. Writing that down forces a kind of clarity that's hard to reach through conversation alone. Vague assumptions become explicit, and explicit assumptions can be challenged before they're expensive to fix. A two-page doc that a colleague reads in twenty minutes can surface a flaw that would have cost two weeks of coding. For small teams, where every engineer's time is a large fraction of total capacity, that trade is especially good.

Everyone holds the whole picture in their heads, decisions get made in hallway conversations, and the code itself serves as the record of what was decided. Then the team grows a little, or a key person takes a two-week vacation, or someone opens a six-month-old module and cannot figure out why it works the way it does. That's when the hidden cost of skipping the design step shows up: the same debate gets had three times, two engineers build competing versions of the same feature, and a rewrite happens that nobody planned for.

A design doc is a short document, often just a few pages, that describes a problem, the approaches you considered, the one you picked, and why. Writing it forces you to answer questions that are easy to skip when you're excited to start coding: What exactly are we solving? What does success look like? What are we deliberately not doing? Who or what will this break? The act of writing often matters more than the document itself, because it turns vague assumptions into concrete claims that others can challenge. A flaw caught in a paragraph costs minutes to fix. The same flaw caught after three weeks of implementation can cost the better part of a sprint, and it is often caught by accident rather than by design.

rows.plain:
# Write the Design Doc First: Why Small Teams Should Plan Before They Code

There is a particular kind of silence that falls over a small team at the start of a project. Someone says, "Let's just start building and figure it out as we go." Everyone nods, because speed feels like the only thing that matters when you have three engineers and a launch date. Two weeks later, the same three people are in a heated thread arguing about whether the API should return IDs as integers or strings, a question nobody thought to settle, and the first version of the feature has already calcified around an assumption one of them quietly made on day one. Small teams are often told that process is for big companies with layers of management. In practice, the opposite is true: a small team has fewer people to absorb the cost of rework, fewer hours to spare, and far less margin for the kind of misalignment that a few pages of writing would have prevented.

A design doc is not a bureaucratic artifact, and it does not have to be a forty-page document reviewed by a committee. At its best, it is a short, shared written answer to a handful of questions: What problem are we solving? What does success look like? What are the options we considered, and why did we pick this one? What are we explicitly not doing? Writing those answers down forces a kind of clarity that is hard to reach through conversation alone. Ideas that sounded complete in a whiteboard session often reveal gaps the moment you try to put them in sentences. And because the document exists before the code, the cheapest place to find a flawed assumption is on the page, not in production, where fixing it means unwinding weeks of work.
rows.steered:
Most small teams skip the design doc. They open an editor, start a branch, and figure out the rest as they go. For a few weeks that feels fast. Then two engineers build the same caching layer in different ways, a feature ships that nobody agreed on, and the first real conversation about the system happens in a code review, after the work is done.

A design doc is the cheap fix. It is a few pages that say what you are building, why, what you considered and rejected, and how you will know it worked. Writing it takes an afternoon or two. Reviewing it takes less time than a single round of rework. For a team of four or five, that trade is usually worth making, even though the process feels heavy at first.

Here's a message you can send your teammate:

---

Hey, the nightly job failed because its IAM role no longer has `s3:PutObject` on the target bucket. Someone changed the S3 bucket policy, and the change removed or overrode the permission the job relies on. The job ran fine before, so the code didn't break. The access did.

To fix it:

1. **Confirm the cause.** Check the job logs for `AccessDenied` on `s3:PutObject`. In CloudTrail, look for denied `PutObject` calls from the job's role around the time the policy changed. Then compare the current bucket policy with the previous version (bucket policies are versioned if the bucket has versioning enabled, or check the Git/Terraform history if that's where it's managed).

2. **Restore access.** Add back a statement that allows the job's role `s3:PutObject` on the required prefix, such as `arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/<prefix>/*`. Also check for an explicit `Deny` that matches the role, since an explicit deny overrides any allow.

3. **Keep it minimal.** Grant only `s3:PutObject` on the specific prefix the job writes to. Avoid `s3:*` or a bucket-wide wildcard.

4. **Prevent a repeat.** Manage the bucket policy in code (Terraform or CloudFormation) so changes go through review, and consider an alert on bucket policy changes (a CloudTrail event on `PutBucketPolicy` works).

5. **Rerun the job** once the policy is fixed, or backfill the missed run if the output is date-partitioned.

Let me know if you want help drafting the policy statement once you've confirmed the bucket and prefix.

---

rows.plain:
Here's a message you could send, followed by the steps to fix it.

---

**Why the nightly job failed**

The nightly job failed with `AccessDenied` on `s3:PutObject`. Someone changed the S3 bucket policy, and the policy no longer grants the job's IAM role permission to write to the bucket. The job's code and IAM role didn't change. The bucket's access rules did, so the role's write was rejected.

**What to do**

1. **Confirm the cause.** Check the job logs for `AccessDenied` on `PutObject`. Then look at the current policy with `aws s3api get-bucket-policy --bucket <bucket>` and check whether the role's ARN still has an Allow for `s3:PutObject` on the target prefix. Use the IAM Policy Simulator to test the role against the bucket if you want certainty.

2. **Find out who changed it and what changed.** Search CloudTrail for `PutBucketPolicy` or `DeleteBucketPolicy` events on the bucket around the time the job started failing. The event shows the caller and the time. If the policy is in version control or infrastructure-as-code, diff it against the last known good version.

3. **Restore write access.** Choose one:
   - If the change was accidental, restore the previous policy. S3 doesn't version bucket policies, so use the IaC repo or the policy JSON captured in CloudTrail.
   - If the change was intentional, add an Allow for the job's role ARN with `s3:PutObject` on the required prefix. Also check for an explicit `Deny` that would override it.
   - If the bucket uses SSE-KMS, make sure the role can also use the KMS key (`kms:GenerateDataKey` and `kms:Encrypt`), or the write will still fail.

4. **Rerun the failed job** once access is restored, and confirm the output landed in the bucket. If the job has a backfill or catch-up mechanism, run it for the missed night.

5. **Prevent a repeat.** Manage the bucket policy in IaC with review, so changes go through a PR. Add an EventBridge or CloudTrail alert on `PutBucketPolicy` for this bucket. Consider a monitoring alert for job failures so a regression like this doesn't go unnoticed overnight.

If you paste the job's error output and the current bucket policy, I can help pin down the exact statement that's blocking the write.
